Our research also shows that a part of the system can exhibit oscillations while the rest remains in a state of flow and we provide a condition for this situation to occur. Our study is performed on two different systems: one made of bosons and one made of fermions, and we find that the phenomenon of bloch oscillations occurs in both systems but with differences depending on the characteristics of the inside structure of these systems. Our research is the first to study the phenomenon of bloch oscillations in systems with a complex energy spectrum and it opens the door to control the flow of particles within these systems through an external acceleration field.

In this study, we explore transitive codes within the context of generalised quadrangles (GQs). A code in a graph is defined as a subset of its vertices that satisfies a specific distance criterion, and it is classified as transitive if it maintains its defining properties when any automorphism of the graph is applied. The code's codegree is determined by the minimum sum of distances between pairs of nonadjacent vertices. Given a GQ Q(q,n), we establish a complete classification for all neighbor-transitive codes of codegree four or higher in Q(5,8) and partially resolve a similar issue for Q(9,16). Additionally, the findings provided shed light on the classification problem for neighbor-transitive codes of codegree four or higher in generalised quadrangles of order two.

A young, dense star cluster called the Arches cluster is located near the heart of the Milky Way galaxy and is surrounded by a dense gas cloud called the Central Molecular Zone. To determine the mass distribution within this cloud, researchers used stellar cluster masses and spatial densities to calculate a two-dimensional correlation function, which suggests a mass anisotropy and a mass radius that is approximately 30 percent smaller than the radius of the area within which the cluster's stars are spread out. This mass anisotropy is consistent with the idea that the cluster's gas cloud is in the process of forming stars.

A comprehensive rate model was developed to simulate an all-around High-Fluence X-ray Absorption Fine Structure (HFXAFs) response, which was compared with the experimental results and with the FEFF9.6 simulation software using a specific gold target. This new model incorporates four inter-atomic correlation parameters, which were determined through a non-linear least squares procedure along with the inner shell ionization rates, inner shell absorption coefficients and time-resolved fluorescence yields that were previously established in research papers. The comprehensive model, with its associated parameters, was validated by its high agreement with both the experimental results and the FEFF9.6 simulation software. In addition to its practical use in data analysis, this new model has the ability to provide insight into underlying physical processes that were not well understood, such as the effect of electron relaxation on high fluence XAFS signals.

This paper outlines the development of a temperaturereferenced detector designed for use in temperature-sensitive applications. The design leverages a pair of PMOS transistors to create a temperature-dependent voltage supply, which is then tracked by a reference voltage that is established through a self-biasing circuit. The detected temperature is determined by comparing the monitored voltage to a predetermined reference temperature, which is implemented using a conventional BMOS temperature sensor. The proposed design boasts an exceptionally wide temperature range of -40°C to 120°C, operates with a low power consumption of 0.8 μW, and features a remarkably tiny 0.06 mm$^{2}$ die area. Additionally, the design offers high measurement precision and a low error margin of merely $\pm$1.4 °C. Furthermore, the design has undergone thorough characterization in a temperature-controlled chamber, and the results show a notable 80°C trigger temperature range between -20°C and 60°C.

Quantum entanglement is a key feature of quantum physics that also holds the potential to outperform classical approaches for various applications, including enhanced sensing capabilities and improved communication efficiency. However, the process of generating and distinguishing entangled states is notoriously challenging. A heralded approach offers a solution by leveraging the trade-off between entanglement creation and differentiation, as it allows for the extraction of entanglement-based correlations upon detection of a signal indicating its generation. This goal is achieved in our experiment by employing a quantum scissors technique that can identify entanglement through direct measurement of a signal, thereby eliminating the need for complex differentiation procedures. By utilizing this Heralded approach, we have successfully created and demonstrated polarization-entangled photons with a high level of accuracy and quantifiable error margins.

This study explores virtual Euclidean spanners: geometric spanners derived from a Euclidean metric space, whose existence is ensured by a famous result of Alon, Carmon, and Krauthgamer showing that any Euclidean metric space with n points has a virtual spanner, a geometric spanner whose stretch factor exceeds the minimum possible value by at most O(log n / log log n). We investigate the computational efficiency of constructing such spanners. In particular, we demonstrate that any virtual spanner with a sublinear bound of O(δ ^ α) on its stretch factor can be efficiently constructed (in linear time) for n-point Euclidean metric spaces. We also establish that the same efficiency can be achieved for constructing geometric spanners, an area of research previously unrelated to virtual spanners. Our results build on a new concept, the spanner number, a measure of how much a stretch factor can be reduced by a geometric spanner, which could be useful for further investigation.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement for security systems to detect potential threats and protect networks.  However, the constantly evolving nature of IoT means that malicious actors can establish a connection to the network the moment a new device is added. Therefore, rapid identification of IoT devices is essential. Fortunately, machine learning can significantly improve the identification speed while reducing the time needed for data collection. Our research focuses on developing efficient methods to extract features from IoT data that takes into account the expenses of these features for accurate modeling, a topic that has received limited attention so far. Our approach, CHAOS, combines exceptional time-efficiency and accurate classification with a low computational cost. CHAOS outperforms leading methods, including DeepNet, EPCNN, and EPCNN-LSTM, by achieving the fastest classification speed, the lowest feature extraction cost, or both, for datasets Ming, OM, and REDESF. Additionally, CHAOS provides extracted features to the leading methods, demonstrating cost-awareness and enhancing their performance.

Godel modal logics can be represented through the lens of bilinear modal logics, which is a subclass of non-distributive modal logics. Godel modal logics exhibit a unique capacity for amortized proof systems, which is a subsystem of substructural logics. This paper explores the transfer of the duality theorem from the original Godel modal logic to its extensions by modal operators. The extensions are characterized by antidistributive relations in their algebraic representations.

A one-shot learning approach for word alignment is presented, which utilizes BERT and a set of sentences from any available translation pair without requiring extensive training. It leverages the pre-trained model's properties and incorporates a simple word comparison mechanism to determine word alignment based on early neural mapping. This method was tested on a German-English corpus and achieved comparable results with the widely used GIZA++ aligner when trained on 550,000 sentence pairs, and even performed better on a smaller dataset consisting of 5,000 sentence pairs. Furthermore, it demonstrated robust performance across various language pairs and enhanced the efficiency of neural machine translation system tuning and hyperparameter optimization.

We introduce a distorted resolvent method to establish the existence of mixed strategies in zero-sum games with continuous and compact graphs, accompanied by a finite number of inequalities. This approach yields insight into the approximate resolution of mixed equilibria and leads to a computational method utilizing smoothing kernels. By analyzing the spectral properties of the distorted resolvent, we investigate the convergence of an iterative algorithm generating mixed strategies, which fails to do so in general. Nonetheless, our findings imply that this algorithm produces epsilon-approximations of Nash equilibria in the limit of epsilon approaching zero.

In this research, Primordial Black Holes are proposed as a potential candidate to explain Dark Energy phenomena due to their low initial densities. Although multiple PBH candidates have been ruled out by various gravitational wave observations, this study investigates the cosmological effects of a hypothetical dark energy-induced scenario where a significant portion of the universe's mass is comprised of PBHs. By utilizing the PopSyCLE simulation tool, researchers analyzed the spatial distribution, matter distribution, and gravitational lensing patterns within this hypothetical universe. Their analysis shows that PBHs significantly affect the galaxy distribution, especially within the range of dark energy mass estimates (10^-12 - 10^-9 MeV). These findings suggest that PBHs could potentially alter the large-scale structure of the universe and may therefore be considered an intriguing alternative to dark energy to be explored in future research.

A comprehensive study focuses on the dynamics of a system consisting of rigid wedges formed by ball collisions, where the impact parameters are chosen to introduce nontrivial angular conditions into the network's structure. In this theoretical work, we examine both the long-term stages of the system's evolution and its short-term behavior, where the interaction between colliding balls results in a damped oscillatory motion due to the imposition of angular constraints. It is revealed that the system's history can be categorized into distinct time intervals characterized by a splay regime, where the distance between colliding stages gradually increases. This time-interval categorization, where the system's dynamics can be described analytically, lays the foundation for a theoretical determination of the system's parameters, particularly its damping coefficient, which is essential for understanding the system's behavior in scenarios where the system's configuration may lead to encounters between balls in a single chaotic orbit.

Several numerical eigenvalue decomposition methods have been developed for approximating the discrete logarithmic derivative of a function on the surface of a sphere. These methods, such as BLAS and the spherical BLAS, apply fast Fourier transforms on a sphere to solve differential equations and calculate Laplace transforms efficiently. However, these methods have limitations when dealing with positive sources in the Fourier sphere problem, which is a fundamental component of the spherical BLAS. We present an innovative approach for calculating discrete logarithmic derivatives directly from a sphere without relying on fast Fourier transforms or matrix decomposition. Our method, which is based on one-step recurrences, provides a simple and efficient solution that outperforms traditional eigenvalue decomposition methods, especially when dealing with positive sources on a sphere.

We introduce a new concept for implementing the quantum visualization technique, the Field Simulation and Measurement Interpretation Tableau (FSMIT), which enables the simultaneous visualization of undetected particles without needing additional detectors. This approach is taken from a previously proposed Friedman-Bunster type experiment and is now developed further to explore the non-absorbed photons in the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state. By incorporating FSMIT, the undetected photon field can be derived directly through measurement outcomes without the need for additional detectors. This model highlights the ability of FSMT to describe both detected and undetected particles within a quantum system. Undetected photons play a significant role in the understanding of the GHZ state and play a crucial role in the development of future quantum applications.

The interaction between complex liquids and solid surfaces is influenced by various factors including surface roughness and the presence of surfactants. When certain liquids come into contact with a solid, adhesion occurs due to intermolecular forces such as van der Waals forces or surface tension, leading to an increase in contact area between the liquid and the solid. However, if the liquid contains surfactants that lower its surface tension, a specific combination of liquid and solid properties can actually reduce the contact area, a phenomenon that can slow down the liquid's flow and increase friction. We have observed this unique relationship between surface tension and friction in liquid foams using force sensors and a stationary surface with irregularities. The presence of dry soap films led to an increase in friction, whereas adding dilute liquid layers caused friction to decrease before increasing again as the liquid films closed over dry soap film patches. The experiments were conducted with different types of surfaces and temperatures, and the findings are explained through a combination of theoretical aspects related to dry soap films and ELR (van der Waals interactions that occur at shorter ranges).

This research presents an accurate deep learning approach to identifying skin cancers from images, with a particular focus on handling diverse data sets. To tackle the challenge of dealing with irregularities in the training data, we utilize the information from multiple classifiers to create a comprehensive probability profile for each image, which helps filter out anomalous samples and yield better classification results. Our proposed method has demonstrated exceptional accuracy on the ISBI 2017 challenge dataset and the original dataset combined with the HAM10000 dataset, achieving a high overall accuracy of 93.75%, with a significant improvement of 6.4% compared to the baseline deep learning model. Furthermore, by incorporating the entropy of the probability profile into the input, our deep learning model is able to achieve a high accuracy of 94.26% on the HAM10000 dataset, outperforming the baseline by 4.1%. Notably, this research presents an efficient deep learning strategy for identifying skin cancers that can effectively handle diverse data sets, featuring a compact architecture of 94 layers and a small memory requirement of 290.52 MB.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Molecular dynamics simulations frequently rely on the propagation of trajectories in phase space, but these trails do not remain confined to a constant initial volume. We introduce a simple method to preserve the constant phase space volume during the dynamics, which is particularly useful for analyzing the phase space structures in jacketed simulations. To illustrate the technique, we examine a system that undergoes free expansion, focusing on the evolution of trajectory spreads, distribution functions, and Hamiltonian paths in phase space.

This paper uses local coordinates to define a specific diffusion equation, which calculates the weights of graph combinations according to Kontsevich's formula, given a symplectic structure with specific properties. We then demonstrate that this diffusion equation has a unique solution, which can be broken down into two distinct components, each having a different level of diffusion impact. We provide a detailed explanation of how the first component interacts with the graph structure, which can be broken down into several distinct aspects, including graph splitting, edge length calculation, and a diffusion process applied to the edges. We also show that the second component only affects nodes of a graph, and provide a general expression for diffusion weights involving multiple symplectic structures, which we then test on a specific example.

We explore nanoptera in two types of weakly nonlinear granular arrays, specifically woodpile and diatomic chains. These special types of chains exhibit Horst states characterized by large amplitude, long-wave solutions. We demonstrate that in both cases, localized and traveling wave solutions can occur, particularly when the granular system possesses a pure repulsive interaction. In contrast, these exotic states disappear in systems with a combination of repulsive and attractive interactions.

A potential primordial feature in the cosmic microwave background spectrum can be generated by particles moving at the speed of light under weak interactions characteristic of a quasi-degenerate spin-zero state, known as traditional cosmological collider physics. It's predicted that massive particles will form early in the universe and quickly decay into lighter particles, resulting in characteristic features in the primordial features, such as a ridge-like structure, that can be generated by a pair of particles moving in opposite directions. This phenomenon has analogies with particle collider physics, where it is referred to as a "golden mode."

An accordion chart is a graph consisting of a complete graph divided by a set of independent edges. This paper explores the properties of accordion charts, including their cycle structure and pairings. By reducing the degree of vertices in an accordion chart through the replacement of edges, it is shown that their structure is equivalent to that of a quartic circulant graph. The equivalent transformation of a Hamiltonian path in an accordion chart to a quartic circulant graph is also demonstrated. Furthermore, an accordion chart is said to have a perfect pairing if its square-free subgraph pairing. This pairing is equivalent to the graph's Hamiltonian path. A perfect pairing accordion chart is isomorphic to a quartic circulant graph with a perfect matching.

We carry out a thorough analysis of the one-dimensional three-state quantum walk's dynamics. The model includes coin states that can evolve according to random matrix theories, similar to the two-state quantum walk case. The general behavior indicates the presence of four distinct dynamic regimes. In the initial time period, the probability density of the walker's position exhibits a Gaussian distribution with a widening spread. At intermediate times, a power-law decay is observed, which transitions to a short-time regime characterized by an exponential decay in the late time period. In addition to observing a smooth, non-oscillating pattern in the walker's backtracking behavior over time, we apply a finite characteristic time to absorb the walker's initial position and coin state dynamics. This reveals a universal, state-independent non-local interference pattern following a long, asymptotic time period.

This paper introduces the concept of self-guided attention in Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures, allowing for the creation of varied training protocols that can enhance model performance and adaptability. By designing a head module to direct signal flow between patch and feature levels, we implement a range of training protocols, from basic to complex, which significantly improve the outcomes across multiple datasets, ultimately resulting in a versatile and effective model. The code for this research is available at: https://github.com/gharpare.

A new cosmological model, known as the Dissipative Combined Dark Fluid model, has been proposed to explain the current acceleration in the universe's expansion. This model introduces a hypothetical dark energy component and a fluid with negative pressure that originates from dark matter due to interactions within a higher-dimensional space. In addition, the model incorporates a dynamic parameter driven by interactions between this dark energy component and matter. Solving the equations, we obtain a non-linear relationship between the universe's age and the scale factor, as well as mathematically defined stages for the universe's phases. Using a least-squares method, we estimated key parameters in the model and found that some of these parameters are consistent with their standard cosmological values, providing a strong indication that the model is viable. Furthermore, we analyzed plots of the quantum states and found that the phases of the universe's expansion, as predicted by this model, align with observed data, including the scale factor's behavior during the late stages of expansion.

We offer a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of H\"older spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, multiple studies have proven that pure noise reduction is insufficient for high-quality image creation, prompting the need for incorporating semantic information into image synthesis. Although notable advancements have been made using continuous promoting variables, they pose significant challenges, particularly difficulty in controlling semantic details and maintaining consistency in output images. Our research presents an innovative approach, the steady creator, combining promoting variables with discrete image features to capture high-level semantic information, resulting in more precise control over synthesized images. Our method starts by creating a creator network to produce an initial image, then uses this baseline to generate a creation schedule with the promotion vector sequence. At each step, the promoter guides the creator with a vector, updating the creator's knowledge by merging promoted semantic information with the current image, through a knowledge injection module, to produce visually plausible and semantically consistent creations. Our technique resonates with the objective of sequential image creation, outperforms existing techniques, and showcases success in various high-level image creation tasks, such as creating sequential chihuahua images from a single image of a chihuahua. Additionally, our technique also produces relevant video content by applying a creator schedule over time.

This research introduces an innovative technique known as reversible concealment that enables a hidden observer to a visual data stream to deduce an underlying target, while ensuring that the associated observations remain confidential. We develop an efficient solution that relies on Bayesian Neural Networks functioning in an adversarial capacity, where the utility of additional data for target inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference inference

Our research investigates the inverse decay process J/psi → (∅ + )invisible from two distinct viewpoints. Firstly, we explored the potential of this reaction to reveal key information about the nature of dark energy, namely its pressure and energy density. Secondly, we examined the relevance of J/psi → (√t + )invisible to neutrino properties as described by effective field theories, including the possibility of non-standard right-handed neutrino interactions. To this end, we collected the most recent data available and performed a global fit to relevant operators within the framework of RGEs, finding that J/psi invisible decays can substantially influence the determination of neutrino properties, particularly if e and μ neutrinos have different masses. Ultimately, our analysis revealed that combining J/psi invisible decays with other experimental constraints can significantly improve constraints on dark energy parameters by approximately 30% and on neutrino parameters representing the ratio of active to total neutrino densities by as much as 300%.

The sun's visible surface is characterized by bright spots, which are hot regions with high surface magnetism, often located near or within the surfaces' characteristic cell structures. To understand the nature of these bright spots, we conducted in-depth observations of a active region containing several of these spots, using a special telescope to measure the areas and shapes of the spots over time. The data revealed that the temperatures within these spots are always higher than their surrounding environments, regardless of location or brightness level. The findings are consistent with theoretical models indicating that the spots are caused by free energy released from moving magnetic fields, which become trapped in the complex network of sunspots. A statistical model, initially applied to the distribution of inbox speeds, provides a accurate fit to the data, and is subsequently used to model the distribution of spot properties, including size, shape, and temperature. The theoretical framework, supported by the observations, suggests that the spots are temporary phenomena, lasting between one and 20 minutes, and are found in areas with high temperatures and strong magnetic fields.

Human vision is remarkably skilled at interpreting short-term motion patterns within low-resolution images, and this ability is essential for everyday life. To comprehensively understand human vision, researchers are exploring the computational mechanisms underlying dynamic identification, although a major hurdle is the scarcity of high-quality training data. This paper overcomes this limitation by leveraging "minimal clips" - tiny, real-world video fragments - to train a deep learning model that surpasses existing benchmarks for predicting motion patterns. The training process yields a compact, generalizable model capable of processing minute videos, and subsequent experiments demonstrate the model's capacity to interpret hidden temporal structures within its input data. Additionally, the study finds that this model is comparable to more sophisticated deep learning architectures in terms of performance.

Theoretical astrophysics offers a unique approach to resolving the conflict between dark matter theories and the fading of galaxy halos' magnetic fields. We have devised a novel model where dark matter is composed of microscopic magnetic monopoles, with the primordial magnetic fields in the universe becoming trapped and preserved from the Big Bang to date. This mechanism operates through the monopoles' inability to annihilate due to the breakage of parity symmetry during cosmological expansion within the galaxy. However, in smaller, local halos like planets and satellites, the lack of parity leads to the release of trapped magnetic energy, causing phenomena such as geothermal activity and the presence of cosmic rays. Furthermore, this model offers a potential explanation for the persistence of galactic magnetic fields, making it a compelling theory to investigate at the microscopic level within the galaxy.

The growing emphasis on climate change requires sophisticated precipitation forecasting. Traditional climate modeling techniques have several limitations, including high computational costs and inaccurate precipitation prediction. Recent advances in deep learning models, specifically CNN-LSTM architectures, have improved precipitation forecasting, but they still struggle with prediction errors, particularly in spatial accuracy. The development of a reliable climate model is crucial for reducing prediction errors. This paper introduces a cutting-edge, 2D-Transformer model called SWCA, built upon a novel cross-attention mechanism, to predict precipitation spatially and temporally. The proposed mechanism, utilizing a sliding window framework, combines precipitation patterns from adjacent regions, aligning them according to the local time of the center grid cell. This is supported by a novel, time-augmented positional encoding, introducing temporal dimensions to grid cell vectors. The proposed model, with its hierarchical structure, integrates local and distant precipitation patterns, often difficult with current climate models. Experiments on the Louisiana precipitation dataset demonstrate that the SWCA model, when evaluated with various metrics, outperforms existing climate models in precipitation forecasting.

In models with three Higgs doubles, we investigate whether the stabilization of dark matter can be attributed to a single mechanism, and if not, we look into the possibilities. Within the framework of the $S_3$-symmetric three Higgs doubles model, a set of numerical results is obtained, taking into account all possible stability conditions, and the feasibility of dark matter with purely geometric stability is examined. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of stability conditions derived from perturbative unitarity and relevance bounds on the dark matter parameters, and highlight two scenarios where the dark matter can exist without any extension to the Higgs portal sector.

In 1998, Wootters showed that a certain condition about entanglement must hold for any composite system, which is known as the PPT triple conjecture. We can make a less restrictive assumption, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis, by considering a simpler scenario. By doing this, we can demonstrate that the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis leads to a complete determination of the entanglement capacity of any composite system, which is known as the entanglement extremal threshold. We can also make another less restrictive assumption, the PPT n-gon hypothesis, which leads to the PPT m-gon hypothesis for any smaller value of m. We can make further generalizations to the n-gon hypothesis in higher dimensions. Additionally, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis can be applied to find the extremal threshold of a key performance metric in a specific type of cryptographic protocol.

In this research, we address the need for an efficient neurological function model that accounts for how neurons control the transport of substances between a cell body and its distant synapses. Our approach diverges from conventional methods, which either simplify the relationship between variables or treat them as uncertain quantities. Instead, we develop an optimization framework that includes partial differential equations to reflect the complex interactions between variables. By viewing the transport process as a flow optimization problem, we can determine the restrictions that govern it and subsequently derive the regulations that govern them. We also introduce a new method to solve the resulting nonlinear programming problem and provide numerical results to demonstrate the efficacy of our model, which offers insights into the mechanisms governing substance transport regulations. Furthermore, we identify a parameter set that solves this optimization problem, thereby shedding light on the parameters that govern neuronal function. We believe that this model will contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex processes involved in neuronal health and disorders such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

The network topology of global financial trade is intricately linked to the flow of money and investment. To gain a deeper understanding, researchers have devised a new metric called Net-Map mOverlaps (NeMo), which is utilized to analyze the interconnections between countries via financial flows and ratings changes. By applying an efficient calculation method, researchers then fish out distinctive patterns in the resulting networks, investigating their implications for financial crisis predictions in the process.

A massive black hole and a white dwarf star are primordial objects that form at the center of galaxies through large-scale gravitational collapse. Their interaction, especially in close binary systems, can result in the white dwarf losing mass, ultimately sinking into the black hole. Such a process is part of a broader category of phenomena known as compact object interactions. In a study, researchers simulated the radiation emitted from a white dwarf as it orbits a massive black hole near the center of a galaxy, similar in size to the Milky Way. Their findings show that a non-axymmetric disturbance of the white dwarf's surface causes fluctuations in the ultraviolet and visible light emitted. These disturbances continue to vary as the white dwarf experiences periodic changes in its distance from the black hole. Through their simulation, researchers determined the potential observability of these disturbances using telescopes on Earth, and found that a significant number of these events could be detected with a telescope of the same sensitivity as the future James Webb Space Telescope. Their work shows that the behavior of the white dwarf and the surrounding disk, or material left over from the disk that the white dwarf is sinking into, can be observed and studied.

The study includes a comprehensive analysis of the baryonic currents formed by three quarks, consisting of light and heavy quarks, within the context of light-cone sum rules. It also explores the possible virtual dressing of these currents by means of mesons and encompasses a thorough examination of the form factors associated with three-quark states, including corrections from mesonic effects. The form factors considered encompass the relevant decay processes of a tau lepton, such as those involving one meson and three quarks, as well as interactions involving two mesons and quarks. The application of light-cone sum rules to these form factors enables a quantitative estimation of the numerical impact of these effects on the baryonic currents and form factors in question.

We present a parametrized family of functions connecting the Jaccard distance to a variant of the normalized entropy distance, offering a general framework for understanding sets' similarity. This metric is shown to adhere to the triangle inequality, making it a valid distance function. By examining the solution set of a specific optimization problem involving the normalized entropy, we analytically derive our proposed distance formula, ultimately illustrating the relationship between this metric and the Jaccard distance through a straightforward expression that relies on the harmonic mean of the distances between two data points.

Existing deblurring methods are primarily designed for still backgrounds, 
but they can't as easily handle time-lapse videos without needing manual 
correction for moving objects. Our research introduces an innovative, 
background-agnostic approach that uses a pseudo-blur generator to analyze 
movement patterns in both people and the scene. This unique system makes 
three key contributions: Firstly, it employs a novel, low-dimensional data 
representation to differentiate moving subject and stationary scene elements 
on a frame-by-frame basis during the blur generation process. Secondly, 
its pseudo-blur generator learns to forecast the blurriness of both humans 
and the scene based on this low-dimensional data. Ultimately, its sequential 
deblurring process uses estimated subject and scene movements to restore the 
original frames. Our experiments show that our method produces higher quality 
results with fewer artifacts compared to existing deblurring methods, and 
it also runs faster, making it more practical for use. Our code is available 
at https://github.com/DeepLearning-Python/HPD_deblurchallenge_editions

We've developed a novel, chemical-based framework called the LFSN Framework, which mimics a neural system using multiple reaction systems. This framework, modeled after a leaky Integrate-Fire neuron, can simulate up to three distinct neural behaviors: action potential generation, adaptation, and spike pattern learning. We've implemented the LFNs using two different chemical reaction networks, one based on a simple kinetic model and another that utilizes complex species. We've tested the feasibility of the LFSN Framework by designing biological motifs with realistic kinetic parameters that match the desired neural functions, and we've evaluated their stability using linear stability analysis and in silico simulations. The results show that both the simple and complex models can effectively support the required neural behaviors, and we believe that the LFSN Framework has tremendous potential for advancing biological computation and synapse design.

In the context of nonstandard analysis, we are working within the hyperreal number system. This study delves into elementary set theory with a focus on arranged sets and their transfinite numbers. A set is considered arranged if it comprises a sequence of subsets that increase in cardinality. The main ideas of this research relate to the absolute continuity of functions between arranged sets, and the development of a specific measure on these sets. The authors also establish a completeness theorem for a specific system within first-order logic. This theorem demonstrates the existence of a model that satisfies a specific formula in a specific system, and can be applied to arranged sets and their transfinite numbers. The proof of this theorem involves a novel approach to the lowenheim-skolem theorem that does not rely on back-and-forth methods.

The growing cost of training Deep Learning models is a pressing concern for organizations. To optimize this process, researchers have long relied on general purpose benchmarking, which compares model architectures on a specific dataset. Yet, recent advancements in hardware and software have created opportunities for more personalized approaches. In our research, we demonstrate the effectiveness of dataset-specific profiling, a method that focuses on evaluating the unique characteristics of a dataset to inform model optimization. Our findings, guided by theoretical modeling and supported by experimental results, show that benchmarking alone is insufficient for optimizing training Deep Learning models. Additionally, the most efficient methods of dataset profiling depend closely on the dataset's features. Our empirical analysis verifies the feasibility and precision of our proposed profiling methods, yielding significant improvements in inference latency, throughput, and energy consumption, in cases where batch sizes vary greatly.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that if the chromatic number of a given graph increases by $k$ or more, it contains a complete graph of order $k$. This has been verified for specific graph types, yet the issue remains complex for certain others. We found that particular 4-color and 5-color graphs comply with Hadwiger's conjecture, which implies that if the conjecture is true, the result holds for all 5-color graphs, while the result holds for all 4-color graphs with clique sizes exceeding 4. Our proof involves reducing the chromatic number of a given 5-critical graph by at least 5, or its 4-critical counterpart by at least 4, after removing a complete graph from it, which corresponds to a question answered in the affirmative by Erdos and Pippenger for 5-critical graphs, but the new result holds for 4-critical graphs as well.

This research presents an innovative, robust adaptive algorithm for recovering smooth graph signals, utilizing a generalized correntropy-based metric that's effective in handling non-Gaussian noise. A specific optimization approach has been developed to determine the kernel width, enabling the metric to converge effectively. By leveraging the optimization technique, the proposed algorithm converges rapidly to achieve high precision in recovering the signal. Notably, the algorithm's computational complexity has been analyzed and found to be comparable to existing methods. Experiment results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm in terms of signal restoration performance and computational efficiency.

Research focused on the generation, analysis, and application of highly entangled quantum states at the micro- and nanoscale is crucial for understanding the behavior of these complex systems and improving their measurement capabilities. A specialized device known as the entangled spinor interferometer is used to create and study these quantum states through diffraction and induction processes. By utilizing this device, researchers are able to create customized quantum states based on entangled electron spin states, which are then diffractioned and collected as distinct spin states at detectors. Through a combination of diffraction and induction capabilities, the state of the system can be manipulated and modified. To overcome detection limitations, the entangled quantum state is optimized such that its diffraction pattern remains unaffected by detection inaccuracies, essentially remaining unchanged regardless of errors at the detectors. This optimized state is then used to set a detection standard, effectively accounting for detection noise to provide highly accurate measurements. Computational tools, including a customized Python script, help researchers design and simulate the entangled quantum states produced by the device, as well as analyze and modify these states through numerical simulation.

The focus of this research is on estimating the initial Robin eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator. This study demonstrates that its approximation can be refined by taking into account higher-order terms of a related nonlinear problem, under specific assumptions. This result extends a previous finding by Levithan and Zelditch, who had shown that the initial eigenvalue could be estimated by considering a first-order approximation. Unlike existing literature, which focused on approximations near the eigenvalue itself, this work delves into the precision of eigenvalue approximations of higher orders.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have become a valuable tool for localized graph transformations, with extensive applications in sociology, social media monitoring, and computer vision. Researchers have explored graph convolution (GC) operations in multiple perspectives, yet the underlying principle of GC remains unclear. particularly, the interconnection between GC and traditional signal processing concepts is not well understood. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by revealing the hidden graph convolution kernel through a matched filtering approach, providing visual insights into the GC process. In doing so, we relate the matched filter framework with historical radar and signal processing technology, offering a modern application. The findings illustrate how the limited support of the graph convolution kernel enables data propagation along graph edges, utilizing signal values at adjacent nodes. Our analysis demonstrates that the GCNN's ability to learn meaningful patterns relies on the input graph's topology and node attributes. We corroborate these findings with numerical experiments using diverse graphs, focusing on the unknowns of unsolved problems and highlighting their intrinsic connections.

Recent advancements in neural models have demonstrated the ability to learn complex dependencies with minimal training data, yet the vast majority of languages remain under-resourced. A significant challenge lies in the scarcity of sufficiently annotated data for supervised learning. This paper introduces a novel, self-training method called Deep Contextualized Auto-training, combining contextualized fast neural feed-forward neural networks with iterative self-supervised learning techniques to effectively utilize abundant unlabeled data for dependency analysis in resource-scarce languages. The proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on four under-resourced languages, achieving impressive results that match the performance of traditional, supervised models trained on large datasets.

We've analyzed the semileptonic decay processes of $B$ mesons transitioning into $D$ mesons, considering the role of light quarks within the bound state. By applying light-front quantization principles, we've developed a quark model that respects both $SU(f)$ symmetry and $C$ and $P$ symmetry. The model allows the calculation of transition form factors at various momentum fractions carried by the light vector mesons, and our findings align well with experimental data and other theoretical model predictions on light-front quark-diquark and instanton-induced scenarios. The results obtained demonstrate the importance of including the effects of light quark mass differences in the bound state wave functions to achieve a form factor accuracy of 5-10%. Furthermore, using our form factor results, we've updated the $m_c(B^0)$ meson mass measurement and the $|V_{cd}/V_{cs}|$ quantity, yielding $m_c^{BF}=(2.613\pm0.008_{\rm theory}\pm0.006_{\Delta\kappa})$ MeV, within 1 MeV of the current world average, and $|V_{cd}/V_{cs}|=0.15\pm0.03$ with an uncertainty of about 20% at the 1 sigma confidence level.

Light elementary particles with unusual properties might be freely exchanging between membranes in 3D boson fluids models. To study these scenarios, we investigate the behavior of particles confined within a fixed sphere under the influence of a high-frequency and irrotational external flow. It is assumed that the fluid on the surface of this sphere has a 3D free Bose gas as its origin. This research includes calculating the changes in the chemical potential and the pressure within the sphere as it adapts to an increased temperature. Additionally, we consider a situation in which particles on one side of the sphere can be moved to the other side, but with a change in their statistical state, effectively inverting their state. This research provides equations governing the diffusion of these particles under an external flow and highlights the impact of inverting the particle's state on this process. Finally, we present plots illustrating how the particle's state inversion affects its diffusion, showing a significant slowing down when the particle's state is inverted.

We establish a relationship between the class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by nonuniform algorithms and those solvable in O(n^k) time by uniform algorithms, indicating that the latter is not significantly more efficient than the former. To demonstrate this, we first show that any decision problem solvable in O(n^k) time can be solved in polynomial time when given additional linear space. We then establish a tighter bound, stating that these two classes are equivalent regardless of the amount of space provided. Our proof builds on a previous result by Karp and Lipton, and is also connected to a conjecture by Valiant concerning the closure of P. We also discuss the impact of our findings on the study of polynomial-time algorithms with symmetric inputs. Furthermore, our tightens a previous result by Blass, Gurevich, and Levenson, and allows us to conclude that a conjecture held by Cai, Furer, and Immerman can be resolved uniformly. We present a simpler proof for a crucial lemma initially established by Paul and Raz, and use this to show that our result does not rely on the acceptance complexity of the complement problem. Finally, we present two applications of our result, one concerning symmetric problems and another involving the solvability of trilinear equations in fields with three elements.

In the pyrochlore iridates, a series of compounds with the chemical formula Eu_1-xBi_xIr2O7, exhibiting insulating to metallic phase transitions, have been studied using a novel high-energy photoemission spectroscopy technique called Hard X-ray Photoemission Spectroscopy. This method enabled us to analyze the insulating to metallic phase transition within the bi-ion series. Our analysis reveals a significant increase in the binding energy of the insulating state at bi-ion concentrations of 0.75, corresponding to a the activation energy of the insulating state. Our findings can be attributed to an insulating to metallic phase transition facilitated by local distortion of the bi-ion's d-electrons, inserting electrons into the insulating state, and our observations are in agreement with theoretical predictions utilizing a 5d tight-binding model.

We establish a two-dimensional set-valued mapping, called Lipschitz, which includes a wide range of low dimensionally defined set-valued mappings such as Lipschitz multimap and mapping with a bounded Haudorff dimension. The definitions of Lipschitz selection and its equivalent forms are examined. It's proven that for a low dimensionally defined set-valued mapping to be Lipschitz, it's equivalent to having a selection with a bounded Haudorff dimension. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between Lipschitz dimension and other forms of dimension for a low dimensionally defined set-valued mapping. The standards of existence for a low dimensionally defined set-valued mapping to have a Lipschitz selection are established and discussed. Moreover, we analyze the efficiency of various methods for finding a Lipschitz selection, including those that work reliably in specific situations and have no guarantee in general cases, as well as the methods for finding a selection with the least Lipschitz dimension among a set of mappings.

Loose and tight bounds are established for the probability of circular (Kramer) sequences generating transitive or non-transitive sets of permutations, along with specific probability values for certain small n sizes.

A compelling case can be made that the complexity of software engineering is a major obstacle holding advancement in software development back. A particular area where improvement can be made is in the complexity of setting up code, a step that currently demands a considerable amount of time and effort. A particular strategy, known as Quasi-Randomization, offers potential solutions by translating a high-level description of set-up information into a programmable form that can be determined dynamically. Although this approach provides great flexibility in terms of set-up possibilities, it also comes with the cost of significantly increased complexity. In this study, we investigate a more simplified version of Quasi-Randomization, known as Partially Quantized, which imposes a predetermined structure on the possible set-ups in exchange for lower complexity while still maintaining a considerable level of flexibility. A compilation-time analysis tool was developed to study the bounds of complexity for PRM execution and an experimental validation was carried out by comparing PRM with a traditional approach on a real application, which revealed promising results and encouraged the use of PQR as a general framework for optimizing complex systems across computing devices and methodologies.

Light dark matter interacting with nuclei in a small volume can be directly identified through the measurement of the resulting recoil energy of the nuclei. However, in experiments involving dark matter detection, the primary limitation is the inability to distinguish between the signal created by the dark matter and the abundant background radiation present. In certain cases, the interaction of dark matter with nuclei leads to the breaking of a nucleon into a charged pion and a neutral kaon, which has distinct characteristics compared to the standard nuclear interactions. Notably, this process produces an electrically charged final state, thereby allowing for the separation of the dark matter signal from background noise through the use of electric fields to direct and identify the moving charged particles. Specifically, we propose that the measurement of the curvature of the pion's path or the minimum distance between the pion and the kaon can serve as indicators of the sub-GeV dark matter signal, which would be resistant to background interference. Furthermore, we estimate the potential for discovery that can be achieved with future detectors having volumes of 30 and 300 liters.

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, specifically focusing on the Rabi oscillations, entanglement, and photon transmission properties. The initial analysis showed that the Rabi oscillations and entanglement behavior exhibit contrasts when compared to the conventional Jaynes-Cummings model. The anti-Jaynes-Cummings model displays distinct Rabi oscillation patterns and entanglement levels, which are influenced by the detuning and coupling strength. Notably, the detuning parameter plays a significant role in the entanglement generation in this model. Moreover, the investigation revealed that the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model is capable of transmitting information over long distances, with the transmission rate being enhanced by the detuning parameter. The study also confirmed that the optimal transmission rate in this model is significantly higher than that achieved with the Jaynes-Cummings model.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from complex signals is challenging, especially when signal quality is poor. Research has shown that deep learning methods can effectively use information from remote leads to estimate IBIs, but previous studies using ECG signals with low signal-to-noise ratios were limited. Our novel approach presents a complex deep learning model, Tiramisu, that estimates IBIs from ECG signals with low quality and high levels of noise. When tested on the MIT-BIH database, this method showed the lowest mean absolute error compared to other studies, with an error rate of 14.15 ms. Furthermore, when applied to authentic wearable devices data, the model demonstrated high accuracy in estimating IBIs. This research innovates in two key areas: first, assessing the effectiveness of deep learning methods for EASI leads, and second, using real-world data from wearable devices to estimate IBIs.

We analyze the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) model, which is an extension of the run-and-tumble particle (RTP) model, having introduced a new labor variable to account for energy levels in self-driven particles. In low labor scenarios, the AOUP behaves similarly to RTP, exhibiting a non-thermal, quasi-equilibrium state. However, in high labor conditions, the AOUP exhibits faster movement and a higher persistence rate compared to RTP. Additionally, the probability distribution of the AOUP's position no longer follows a Gaussian pattern as labor levels increase, resulting in a power law dissolution pattern. Increasing labor levels result in the AOUP moving away from its original position more quickly, resulting in a shift in the phase diagram from a non-thermal to a thermal regime.

We present HUMBI, a large, diverse dataset consisting of 54,676 human body gesture
sequences captured from multiple viewpoints, each accompanied by semantic information.
Current state-of-the-art gesture representation methods perform best on in-house datasets.
They tend to produce static, view-specific representations that fail to account for varying
gaze directions or multiple viewpoints, or struggle with encoding complex gesture patterns.
We address these limitations by developing a new benchmark, the HUMBI Challenge, which
poses significant challenges to existing methods. The challenge requires incorporating
gaze and motion data, handling multiple views, and generating expressive, semantic
representations capable of differentiating intricate gesture patterns. We propose two
benchmark tasks: evaluating the generalization of gesture representations to novel
gaze directions and unseen viewpoints, and the performance of these representations
in discriminative tasks. We invite the community to participate in the HUMBI Challenge.

Despite the growing need for NLP models in non-English languages, the limitations in NLP data and computational resources make it impractical to train them independently. Previous research has shown that sharing NLP models across languages is a viable option, with the potential to improve all parties involved. The challenge, however, lies in providing sufficient supervision for language-specific fine-tuning, which is often in short supply. This paper presents a novel approach to cross-lingual transfer for NLP tasks, using neural task representations as weak supervision for learning task-specific models across different languages. The experiment demonstrates state-of-the-art results on 14 out of 16 NLP tasks across 10 languages, highlighting the efficacy of this method. The code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/nyu-vl/TL.

A landmark video super-resolution technique known as BasicVSR has set a new standard for the field, yielding the best results in the VSR challenge at the ICCV 2021, surpassing other top-in-class models. This success is attributed to BasicVSR's efficient 4-division parallel architecture, achieving exceptional video super-resolution results with high quality and efficiency. However, the original approach has several shortcomings that hinder its performance, such as an overly simplistic propagation method, inadequate feature alignment, and a suboptimal decoder design. We developed a series of improvements to these aspects, incorporating them into a new model, BasicVSR++, which demonstrates a substantial improvement over the original model. BasicVSR++ outperforms BasicVSR by a significant margin, and even surpasses several top-performing models in the VSR challenge. The source code for BasicVSR++ is publicly available at https://github.com/Dr0pS0n4ry/BasicVSR.

In a learning environment with limited information, decision-makers are prone to making incorrect choices due to uncertainty, leading to subpar task performance.  While experience helps, it's often insufficient, prompting multi-task reinforcement learning (MLRL) to emerge as a potential solution, leveraging common task patterns to improve outcomes.  However, MLRL's performance can be hindered by competing task goals and information overload.  Our study reveals that in the context of multi-task reinforcement learning, a modular learning system can avoid these issues by focusing on distinct task components, thereby avoiding destructive interference.  Through experiments in both gridworld settings and the game of self-driving with other cars, we observed a modular system capable of learning separate representations for each task, resulting in better performance and reduced time to achieve task goals, compared to a unified learning approach.

Working in complete and finite-time thermodynamics, we investigate the performance of an ideal heat engine when some of the thermal connections become operational for a limited time. The scenario in which all thermal connections are active but not controlled by working fluid is also examined, with its results compared to the maximum efficiency possible given fixed piston and boundary thermal resistances. The case considering an ideal heat engine applies to any type of working fluid. The study's main findings are presented graphically for both the quasi-static and quasi-equilibrium regimes. The calculations are performed using a three-level system where the working fluid interacts with two heat baths of temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$, with $T_1 > T_2$. The measurements of heat provided and work performed by the engine during the finite-time process are described in terms of the temperatures, a characteristic time duration $\tau$, and the temperature difference $\Delta T = |T_1 - T_2|$ that arises due to the engine's operation. The behavior of the system's performance in the finite-time regime is found to significantly differ from that in the quasi-static, finite-duration regime, with the latter being characterized by a temperature relaxation length $L_T$ and a temperature-dependent Prandtl number $\text{Pr}$.

This research addresses the critical issue of protecting power systems from severe hurricane storms. To minimize economic costs associated with system damage, we evaluate areas of high energy risk, aiming to reduce exposure to extremely hazardous events. By combining geographical information with statistical analysis and visualization, we identify high-energy-risk regions that can inform utility companies' strategic planning for system reinforcement or relocation. Our study focuses on the Gulf Coast of the United States, an area particularly prone to catastrophic hurricane storms that can cripple power systems, leaving communities in darkness.

This study establishes a complex theorem known as the three spheres theorem for monogenic functions within Clifford analysis. Specifically, we demonstrate that a non-linear function undergoing Clifford differentiation will remain homogeneous if it exhibits certain symmetry properties when subjected to differential operations. Consequently, its spatial derivatives will also display these same symmetry characteristics. Building upon this outcome, we derive a corresponding result for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator, where the involvement of a linear function is a prerequisite for deriving eigenvalues and corresponding eigenfunctions in this context.

We develop entropy-based approachability theory for a class of games involving simplex trajectories. By incorporating the properties of max-plus polynomials, we generalize the existing theory from linear to nonlinear scenarios. This involves deriving new formulas for the success set of games in terms of the eigenvalues of relevant matrices, and establishing that the eigenvalues follow a specific pattern in nonlinear multi-player games. We demonstrate that the entropy rate of the success set converges to a specific value in many situations. Additionally, we apply our theoretical findings to study the long-term behavior of trajectories in nonlinear systems, such as random digraphs and networks, and examine the implications for the entropy rate. One of the key outcomes of our research is the discovery that the entropy rate of some nonlinear systems, like the Dyck system, fails to exist or is not approachable. We explain this phenomenon by analyzing the connection between the entropy rate and the direction of simplex trajectories, and illustrate that the non-uniform Dirac measure plays a significant role in this relationship.

In a variety of scenarios, such as multi-Higgs potentials or dark energy models, the standard enhanced scalar sector might require attention. Following the Higgs discovery, the focus has been on fitting data with minimal extensions, but future experiments hold the key to revealing characteristics of an enlarged scalar sector. In particular, combined analyses of Higgs coupling measurements, plus advanced sensitivity in precision electroweak measurements and particle collider searches, will likely play a crucial role in uncovering this sector's structure. This could be achieved through a comprehensive analysis that incorporates numerous theoretical models, starting with the most straightforward ones. In this paper, we will explore the potential of future experiments to reveal characteristics of an enlarged scalar sector.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of context in WN using single-time input samples leads to difficulties in modeling spectral patterns across multiple time scales. WN's pitch control is also restricted to a single pitch value per time frame. To address these limitations, QPNet utilizes multiple time frames for the encoder and pitch classifier, and integrates Class-Conditioned Spatial Temporal Dilated Convolution (CCSTD) to refine WN for pitch control. CCSTD's success in generating quasi-periodic signals with precise pitch control is a crucial prerequisite for generating high-quality speech and music signals. CCSTD's performance is, however, sensitive to the choice of the number of conditioning classes and data variability. To address these challenges, QPNet implements a discrete pitch distribution as a soft label for the pitch classifier, making the model more adaptable to different applications. Additionally, QPNet uses multiple conditioning Class-Conditioned Spatial Temporal Dilated Convolution blocks to generate signals with multiple pitch values in a single time frame, increasing the efficiency of autoregressive decoding. Our experiments involve evaluating the effectiveness of QPNet using F-score metrics on both the Timit database and the VCTK speaking in chorus dataset. The results

Latent factor models are the preferred method for recommender systems, cooperating with user and item factors to predict preferences. While cooperative filtering methods can learn user and item patterns, they don't effectively handle cases where only part of a user's preferences are known. Our proposed bicluster-based cooperative filtering method uses CF coefficients as weights for user and item biclusters, leveraging their structure to handle sparse cases. By incorporating user and item specific factors, our method outperforms existing methods, particularly on New York Times data sets.

The sun's active health affects Earth's climate and variable stellar magnetic activity has implications for exoplanet detection and characterizing phenomena in solar systems. Investigating the sun's magnetic activity is essential, and a recent study utilized sun-like stars' data from the HARPS-N solar telescope to investigate the sun's spectral behavior. The research focused on identifying new activity indicators by analyzing the sun's spectral time series, and it revealed that several features are influenced by the sun's complex magnetic activity. Specifically, the research identified 12 new features that show variation in response to the sun's cycle, and it discovered that 5 of these features have a detectable daily oscillation component. These features provide valuable information about the sun's magnetic activity and could be useful for monitoring the sun's activity or that of sun-like stars.

To confidently identify Majorana modes, which are a type of non-local, topologically-protected quasiparticle, researchers need to develop effective methods for detecting them. A key challenge is differentiating Majorana peaks from other types of peaks that may appear in the same measurement. We suggest a new technique that could help achieve this differentiation by utilizing a combination of tunneling spectroscopy and omic damping in measurements conducted by resistive electrodes. This approach will be crucial in making precise predictions about the current progress in nanoscale measurements.

An extension of topological Markov processes to categories with morphisms represents a significant area of study in modern research. The concept of expanding topological Markov chains, which are used to model dynamical systems, into topological categories has been an essential objective. An important discovery in this field is the realization that the transition matrix of such chains can be viewed as a functor that maps the phase space to a directed category, which is a free category with a finite number of generators. The image of the phase space in this category constitutes the set of states of the dynamical system. An essential property of topological Markov chains is the fact that they possess unique states, which are characterized by the fact that the image of the state does not change under the action of the transition matrix. The transition matrix of a topological Markov chain can be viewed as an functor from a phase space to a category of paths in a finite number of generators, which is a free category. The shape of the phase space, which determines its structure, is reflected in the structure of the category of paths, which constitutes the set of states of the dynamical system. The shape of the phase space can be reconstructed from the state of the system by a process that involves a categorical version of the system's development. The category of topological Markov chains contains objects that can be viewed as shadows of finite topological spaces, which are characterized by the fact that the transition matrix maps them to a terminal object in the category

Existing image enhancement techniques are primarily centered around achieving a specific goal, such as restoring a low-quality image or replicating a particular style. In contrast, this study focuses on transferring styles from one high-quality image to another, with a goal of producing a single output that accurately represents both the original low-quality picture and the transformed high-quality image. To accomplish this, a novel approach is developed that extracts a style from a reference image and applies it to the input image through a series of nonlinear transformations. Unlike conventional style transfer methods, the style extraction process in this context involves reversing the direction of style transfer. Specifically, a high-level neural network is trained to directly map a low-quality image to a high-quality one, with a auxiliary reference image providing guidance on the transformation. While the style extraction process is influenced by a reference image, the quality of the output picture solely depends on the input low-quality image. Moreover, the study introduces a universal forward tone mapping network (UfNet) that takes a low-quality image as input and produces a high-quality output, as well as a universal reverse tone mapping network (UrNet) that accomplishes the opposite task. By training these models on a massive dataset containing images of various genres and formats, including MNIST and CIFAR-10, the research demonstrates that the quality of the output high-quality image can be evaluated systematically using metrics such as frequency, multi-scale structural similarity, and fidelity. Ultimately, the quality of the generated high-quality image can be optimized through

This technical report outlines the rules and data description of the AQTC (Approximate Quality of Service via Timed Constituent) task, which is part of the LOVEU challenge entered in the 2022 Computer Vision Pattern Analysis and Machine Learning conference. The report provides an detailed explanation of the AQTC task, including the formation of tuples and the criteria for ranking, as well as the data sets used for training, evaluation, and testing. Additionally, the report describes the evaluation metrics and presents the results obtained from the first round of the competition.

We present direct evidence supporting the theory of preferential selection during snowfall, demonstrating how smaller snowflakes choose to cluster around larger ones in the atmosphere. Our research reveals the details of this process by analyzing snow growth in a laboratory setting using dual-scalar imaging techniques. The findings show that larger snowflakes tend to gather in areas with low rotation rates and high water content, typically created by the accumulation of smaller snowflakes. This preference for larger neighbors is consistent across a wide range of snowflake sizes. Additionally, the study finds that larger snowflakes tend to avoid high-rotation areas with low water content. The competition for growth in the atmosphere favors snowflakes with sufficient time to accumulate around others, explaining the prevalence of larger snowflakes in the atmosphere. The discovery of this preferential selection process sheds new light on the understanding of snowflake development and atmospheric turbulence.

This research presents an application of active inference to roam a virtual 2D space as an independent robot, discovering and mapping out locations that are of interest, such as landmarks, while adhering to safety guidelines. The theory adopts a profound approach, leveraging a vast, unstructured net of credences akin to those utilized in deep learning. The results demonstrate that robots navigating this simulated environment using a straightforward credence update method tend to get stuck in an 'exploration explosion' scenario, typically avoided in more predictable prediction scenarios. However, we identify a novel direction for credence update that enables more balanced exploration and navigation.

In the field of particle physics, event data from detectors like the LHCb are increasingly overwhelming experimental teams. To tackle the resulting storage and analysis challenges posed by the growing data sets, the RICH project has focused on developing lossless and lossy data compression methods for 3D sparse data. Given that the current methods don't fully meet the needs of the LHCb's Trigger Processor System, we've introduced a dual convolutional autoencoder architecture. This innovative approach not only achieves higher compression ratios than existing methods but also evaluates the sparsification level of the data, enabling it to be tailored to the requirements of the Trigger Processor System.

Utilizing the Finzi gravity model, we've obtained a self-consistent equation for the radial density distribution of galaxy clusters. We then compared our results with the Navarro-Frenk-White model by calculating the resulting beta profiles and conventional analysis parameters such as concentration-mass relations, and seed mass estimates based on the concentration-mass relations. We discovered that the beta parameters derived from the Finzi model are comparable to those of the NFW model, yet the predicted concentration-mass relations and seed mass estimates are distinct. We claim that the discrepancies between the two predictions arise primarily from the differing radial density profiles of the two models, specifically the differing radial accretion rates. We verified that the beta parameters are closely tied to the radial accretion rates, which in turn are determined by the specific gravity model in use. We suggest that the NFW-based theoretical predictions of concentration-mass relations and seed mass estimates may not adequately describe the observed trends in galaxy clusters, and that the Finzi model is a potential alternative.

A type of geometric hypergraph called d-dimensional convex geometric hypergraph, PGHd(n), consists of a collection of d-dimensional convex subsets, where each subset contains at least one element. This study explores a problem related to the saturation number of PGHd(n) using a combinatorial approach and provides an upper bound which is nearly optimal in dimension one, with the goal of understanding the general case.

To establish a connection between nuclear mass and other fundamental properties, researchers use the relative $\alpha$-sparse property of nuclear energy density functionals. However, this connection is challenging to establish because $\alpha$-cluster models are generally non-relativistic and difficult to relate to relativistic nuclear energy density functionals. Our recent research introduced a concept of the $\alpha$-generation operator, which can be applied to construct various $\alpha$-cluster models. We have now refined this operator and applied it to the study of $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V rotational excitations. Our results show that the newly refined operator agrees well with other methods and can be used to establish a connection between nuclear mass and other fundamental properties.

A previously (2019) described snake-like robot was a scaled-up version of a robot designed for searching through debris fields. The upgraded robot incorporated a novel locomotion method derived from an analysis of the movements made by a moray eel. The new mechanism allows a robot with four degrees of freedom to move about in any direction, using only two actuators, thus improving efficiency. A simulation of the eel's movement, called "Slinky," was created to study the dynamics of the robot's movements, and test the efficacy of an integral controller. Successful tests of the Slinky simulation, performed in the Unity game engine, showed that it could achieve a high movement speed and mobility in three dimensions, capabilities that are hard to replicate with typical walking or running gaits.

We develop a novel model to analyze colon cancer progression and the immune system's response with its inherent variability considered. By integrating the modeling uncertainty with the inherent variability, we establish a customized treatment strategy that minimizes cancer growth while protecting the patient's overall health. Furthermore, our model accounts for immune system activation and the side effects of treatment, considering the potential for future cancer recurrence. Utilizing the Feynman-Voronin formulation, we reformulate our custom treatment strategy as an optimal control problem, capable of being solved.
